title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06

blocks.x: Okay, we're at the Hogan Jazz Archive and it is April 6, 1992. I'm Bruce Rayburn and we're going to be talking to two New Orleans musicians, Bill Huntington and Charles Suhor. And so why don't we begin with Mr. Huntington and you could give us your name for voice check for the record, date of birth, place of birth and then Mr. Suhor.
My name is Bill Huntington. I was born October 2, 1938 at Turo Infirmary in New Orleans.
I'm Charlie Suhor, born June 3, 1935 at Hotel Jew in New Orleans.
Great. I thought we'd begin with maybe discussing...
All right, Bill, you were, I think, discussing the nonchalance of New Orleans towards this music. Maybe you want to pick that thread up again and amplify a little bit about it.

Well, I always felt, as you said, there was a certain indifference to music here as a profession. I mean, even to this day, people will look at somebody like me. I'm a middle-aged, older, middle-aged man, and people will look at me and say, you know, it's not like I'm a professional. It's like I play with a band, but what is your real job? You know, I mean,
I haven't heard that in a while, but I'm sure.
And if you want to ask me something, Andy Bagger.

Okay, we're into reel two now of Bill Huntington and Charles Sewer. Charlie, maybe you want to amplify a little bit of, now that we've begun to discuss some of the modern jazz players from the 50s and 60s in New Orleans.

Yeah, I won't try to talk about the many, many, but the few who struck me at least as being those who others looked up to as normative, as the real innovators during that time. I guess this spans a period of about 10 to 15 years, and every individual will have maybe a slightly different list, but almost any list I think would have to include Ed Blackwell, who I mentioned before, just an amazing innovator. I'd include also Bill, as I mentioned on the previous reel, Miles Bernadde, a very important figure among the white musicians in the quarter. He just was the head of a clique of mouse worshippers, including my brother Don, who was greatly influenced by his alto, really an original player. He played soprano sax, too. For me personally, I had to put Errol Palmer on there, older than Blackwell, and a really gifted player who since went to the West Coast and was doing very well as a studio musician. He used to play at the Texas Lounge, remember, and other places on Knows Street. I just did a gig with him.
Really?
How wonderful.

Or you can talk about venues, too, so we can get some feeling of where modern jazz players might have been able to play. How exceptional it was for them to get in front of the public. Were they playing for themselves? Were they playing for general audiences? Right.

A lot of that stuff is chronicled on record in the sixties in my Down B columns, which I'll be donating shortly, so that you'll have the venues, the artists, and changes in personnel. Of course that doesn't give you the interpretive stuff and who were the spiritual and musical leaders. Yeah, that's important. So Mouse played in little quarter dungeons, little back rooms and quarters and places like that. Blackwell we used to have a place called Dante's Inferno in the quarter, and little jazz clubs, Holes in the Wall. This was the beat generation time, so it's hip to have a dingy little place. Anyway, Earl Palmer was playing at the Texas Lounge on Canal Street with Earl Williams I think it was. Raw Montreil. Red Talon. Red Talon. Ed Frank, great piano club with the group.
Another great innovator. Yes. Very important, very important guy.

So these are the people who I think others looked up to greatly as musical leaders. Nat Perillat, who died young, was a tenor saxist who people looked up to greatly. I didn't hear Ellis much in those days, not until the mid-fifties. He was in the Marine Corps. Is that why? Okay. But I mean the guys used to tell me, people like Richard Payne, you say, well we always get to get to Ellis' house and he said Ornette Coleman was there, you know, things like that.
Ellis was playing more tenor then actually. The first time I heard him he was playing tenor. I didn't know that. He was a very good tenor player.

Somebody I should mention just because he is sort of a grandparent-like link with so many of the players of the time is a drummer named Lou Dillon, who's now the retiring business agent. He was a damn good teacher. He played some jazz well, played Latin music, played show drums, a good show drummer. But he taught Reed Vaughn when Reed was just kind of bumping around trying to find a style. I know Lou. He's nice. Okay. Reed then said you've got to take lessons from this guy I'm taking from, because Reed was working, just working. You know, and so I went to Lou, a brilliant teacher, and the style of teaching that he did there was so conceptually strong, so encouraging, I think he opened things up for both Reed and me, and I used a lot of his methods when I taught Johnny Vodakovich in Another Generation. You know, so Lou is not known as one of your fire-eating players, but I think he had a lot of influence, at least on the drummers who heard Reed, who I came in contact with, and the drummers who I taught. But anyway, I don't, I mean, what can I say about modern players? John Probst, Joe Mandry, Mike Surpass, Don Seward, Dave West.
Rusty Main, who was an incredible player.

Yeah. But the list, I just wanted to get a sense of my view of who some of the leaders were, who people look to for innovation, you know, perhaps, again, your list might be different, Bill, but I wanted to get that on the table. Sure. Yours.
Oh, okay. Shall I go back to where we left off as far as my background was?
Yeah, why don't you take it?

Okay. Well, anyway, I had started playing tenor guitar, and this whole thing happened with the banjo, and started meeting, you know, it's an interesting thing. I was thinking while I was walking over there, that I had no peer group as a kid. It's very important that you have a peer group, people you grow up with like interests, and you kind of bounce things off of each other, bounce off of each other sometimes. That's important. I didn't really have that, because I was so lonely in this, you know? I mean, the nearest thing to me was, say, Pete Fountain, Ken Collier. And Pete was older than I was, you know. Charlie I didn't know at the time. Don I didn't know at the time. So, I mean, first of all, a lot of people who maybe were interested in this music didn't want to take the chance, or didn't think it advisable to be around black people, period, at the time. And so, I had this such fervor, and I had such an innocence, and maybe like Charlie says, this romanticism, that I just got totally involved and immersed. And I mean, I spent more time with older black people than I did, say, with my own. I'd have to go to school, of course. I'd be in school. But that was it, man. Right after school was out, I did my homework, I was gone. And around that time, I started drinking, unfortunately, too. So, that kind of colors a lot of things that happened to me around that time. I kind of went through a period of seclusion between the ages of, say, 17 to about 19. I was really kind of a recluse. I didn't date, didn't really do the things that a normal older teenager should be doing. Just listened a lot to music, and occasionally, reluctantly went out and did a gig. And that's the reason I think Buddy is so dear to me, Buddy Prima, is because not only did I really appreciate him as a musician, but his friendship was very important to me because he was sort of a bad weather friend, which is the greatest kind of friend that you can, Charlie was that way, too. But Buddy and I lived fairly close together, and Buddy would just take an interest. He would come get me, and he's convertible. And he was so, he had this great sense of humor, man. Right. Very silly, you know, and kind of a show-busy sense of humor. I remember one time, he came with a couple of chicks, and we went out riding. And I mean, he's like, he had this flamboyancy. He's dressed like in this really ridiculous flowered shirt and like Bermuda shorts. And I'm this like reclusive, you know, real dark kid, you know, with sunglasses and a beret. And you know, the beret, I mean, we all, you know, went in for all that. And really kind of like hoaring in the back seat. And we're driving down the middle of Canal Street, and Buddy is like standing up on the seat. Every time the car stops screaming, we are the youth of America! I mean, Buddy Prima's stories are like, they're legion, man. Yeah. But, you know, I mean, we could sit here and just talk for hours about Buddy alone, you know. But he was a very important spiritual influence in my life, and as a friend. And I feel like it's very tragic what's happened to him. I mean, I have to say that. But what an artist. He's an activity. Yeah, such a great, such a great natural artist. He didn't come through. It just didn't come through. It never really materialized for him. For whatever reason, you know, it's not for me to say. But it hasn't.
Very witty singer too, wasn't he? Great, great, yeah.

Ironic, sort of a sardonic singing style, you know. But our involvement during that time is very close, because we played a lot together. And that also helped my development. You know, just playing and being around a person of my own age who was into music. Then I met Charlie through Buddy, met Al Herman, who was a great trombonist. Let's see, who else was in that peer group kind of?

Well, we used to play and Herb Tasson used to come and jam with us at the, at the Premiers Fountain Lounge Club. And a lot of people used to hang around there, because, you know, they liked, we were a rhythm section, and a pretty damn good one. So guys used to come and jam with us, but as far, oh yeah, well. Charlie Miller.

Charlie Miller, who's now living back in New Orleans, is a very, really excellent jazz trumpet player, classical trumpet player as well. And Jimmy Asenheimer, who was a really excellent clarinetist, played with the symphony, and was involved in, Buddy used to have an interesting term for the kind of music we were all kind of getting involved in. We were all getting interested in modern classical music as well. And most of us were studying composition. I had studied for a while with John Butler, who was kind of a guiding light to a lot of musicians around here. An incredible musician who was a doctorate, who had a doctorate from Eastman, who played oboe and piano, had played jazz with people like Coleman Hawkins, you know. And had also, like, done his thesis with Ron Carter playing, like, principal bass. It was an oboe concerto, and Ron Carter played principal on it. So he had been a classmate of Ron Carter's at Eastman. But just this incredible musician who influenced all of us a lot. And Buddy kind of coined this term for the way we were developing. He called it Americana, which was his way of saying the music we were playing wasn't exactly jazz, and it wasn't really classical music. And we were kind of, I guess, for one of a better term, you'd say third stream. But, you know, it was our own outlook. And Buddy was coming up with all kinds of innovative ways of playing. I remember way back then, which was pre-Bill Evans, he came up with the ideas of suspending the rhythm section, not having the bass play a full pulse. And with dealing with, rather than playing a tune the way the tune sounded, with measures, that you would play almost roboto. I mean, he had some very innovative ideas. He was just a very innovative kind of guy, you know, musician. And so that, you know, my playing kind of developed along those lines. And we did this series of radio shows for WWL where we included, Charlie was usually the drummer, and Buddy played piano or trumpet, and I played guitar. The big problem was getting decent bass players. And I think that was part of the reason why I just started developing in the bass. Plus, it was very hard to get to earn a living as a jazz guitarist in the city. And jazz guitar has not been what's been happening here. So if you wanted to play guitar, you wanted to go out to work, you had to play R&B, very much as you have to play rock now. You had to play R&B. And I mean, if you play bum-dum-da-dum-dum-da-dum-dum-da-dum, if you've done that for like five hours, you get tired, it gets tedious. So I mean, I was getting burned out on the guitar. I remember Roy Montrell talking about that very same look, by the way. Roy being one of my early influences on guitar. Great guitar player who died in Germany. Played with Fats Domino. That was his probably greatest gig, but a really good modern jazz guitar player. I remember seeing one time, and this is typical New Orleans kind of venue, driving around by the Magnolia Housing Project, and hearing this great modern jazz, and not knowing where it was coming from, kind of figuring, maybe there's a record store I didn't know about. It was a loudspeaker. And driving, getting closer to the sound, driving these side streets, and finally coming across this, truck. And on this truck was Ed Blackwell playing in the back of a pickup truck. Ed Blackwell, Roy Montrell, Chuck Beatty and Nat Perillot. Playing man. Playing the... The masquerade is over. Just playing man. With the whole sign advertising a gig they were gonna do. That's what they were out there doing. In the afternoon.
That's an old tradition and not usually associated with modern jazz players.

which is typical of the New Orleans experience, that kind of crossover type thing happening. So, and then I did that. Then I started meeting through basically, I guess, working at the Playboy Club. The Playboy Club came along, and Al Boleto created this incredible venue for modern jazz at the Playboy Club, where he had, like, at times, four bands working at the same time. Two quartets and two trios.
It's in the 60s. It's in the 60s. It kind of could end downbeat series very, very clearly.

But, I mean, at the time, you would have some of the very greatest jazz musicians, modernists playing in one of the rooms, you know, and that's where I first met Ellis. There's an interesting story that Ellis has related on a television program recently that he did. And I remember this incident, too. I was playing with a pianist by the name of Eddie Finassi, and Ellis hit a trio with Marshall Smith and James Black, and they were playing upstairs in the room upstairs. And, by the way, Al Boleto was an early integrationist in the music scene and was arrested and beaten for it. You know, I mean, there's an incident that happened where he wanted to play with Earl Palmer and Ed Frank. He and Benny Clementson were both taken in, picked right off the bandstand, taken in. So, I mean, people did get hurt. But, I mean, Al, you know, pushed through having Richie Payne on his band, which was unheard of at the time. You know, you just didn't do that. And this is before, you know, it was really against the law to do that. And then he got Ellis into the Playboy Club, which really wasn't challenging integration laws, segregation laws, but wasn't, you know, I mean, the very fact that we were all together there in the club and meeting each other was an unusual thing socially. So, and in such a public display, a place like the Playboy Club, where everybody's eyes were on that, you know. So, I remember that Ellis came, first I saw, we were playing something, and I saw Marshall Smith over in the corner, and Marshall Smith staring there, looking at me, staring at me. And the next thing I see, he's gone, and he's got Ellis by the arm, and he's bringing Ellis in. He's standing there with Ellis like this. Well, Ellis related to, Ellis says it's like the first time he heard me that Marshall Smith came and got him, and said, you've got to come listen to this guy. It's an interesting story.

So, before you get too far into your bass stuff, I wanted to pick up on something you said about your lack of a peer group when you were with Lawrence Marrero and the black musicians. That was one thing that I think is very unique about you, the fact that of all the players like myself and others who came up with Dixieland as our love, we just didn't have that deep connection with the early traditional players. And it's easier conceptually to pick up the fluff aspects of Dixieland. It's very difficult, it sounds decent, it sounds okay, it's very difficult to pick up the core of the stuff in the New Orleans tradition. And you were unique among us in having that kind of a rootsy connection. And before I knew anything other than your name and you were going to sit in on guitar, and that sounded like a drag to me on a gig once with Buddy Prima. This guitar player comes in, he's setting up and he's playing, and I said, well, guitar players usually get in the way. I said, we're grooving along, and Bill plays the first lick. I said, that is jazz. That's the conception. That's what it is. And later I found out how deep his roots were in it. So I think that's a part of your conception, and it's a part of a unique, fairly unique in the white community in terms of having bridged so many eras in jazz and having had those genuine roots that are so intense. And I value that, and I'd say that if you weren't here, so I wanted to say it now before it got away from me.
Yeah, well, thanks. You know, I don't really know why it happened except that, to me, the older black players embodied what I wanted to hear.
Yeah.

You know, and like I said, it did affect me socially and it affected me psychologically in the sense that for a long time I developed this kind of reaction formation against white music. And I think it's very ironic that as a child I felt this way, and I can see it in so many white people today, which is unfortunate.

Let's get back to something that we mentioned but didn't really go into any detail on it, and that is that integration of the New Orleans Jazz Club stage. You want to give us some detail on who was on that session?

Yeah, I can tell you more exactly how I felt than I could tell you. I can tell you every person who was involved, but I can tell you how I felt. Like I said, by the time, I think I was about 15, I had done the Ken Collier session, so I was probably just about 16. And I remember feeling an awful lot of resentment against what I felt was the white, jazz establishment in the city. That, I mean, being a kid had a lot to do with this because I didn't understand the infrastructure behind the segregation laws and so on. All I understood was, I love these music, I love these people, I mean, these people are great people. Why is it that no one wants to hear them? Why do they have to play in these dives? Why does no one record them? You know, so I kind of took it on myself to be this crusader in my own little way. And one of the things I did was when I started getting involved in the jazz club, I started talking about all the black musicians that I knew, you know, and I decided, I can't remember exactly how I came to this decision or who I talked to, who helped me, but I decided to organize a band and take it up to the jazz club. The band I organized was Sae, Percy, Mealy, and we marched. I don't know how I got these guys to do this, man, but I didn't have any money. I can't imagine paying them anything. But Sae brought it, you can imagine, Sae setting up his drums, Sae Frazier, carrying his drums up to the Roosevelt and everything. And in the interim, like while we were setting up and when we started playing the first tune, George Gerard, there was no bass, George Gerard came up and started playing on the bass, right? And then Jack Delaney, we needed a bone, we didn't have bone. And I liked Jack for whatever reason, I don't know, maybe I just, Jack was a very amicable kind of guy, very sweet guy. And I knew Jack sitting in, but then I remember feeling, and it's funny, if you see the picture, I'm very sullen in the picture. And I remember thinking, this has turned into like chocolate milk, man. I mean, this is an Oreo cookie. You know what I mean? This is what I wanted to say. I wanted to say, listen to these cats play, now it's all getting diluted. I remember that going through my mind, which is really weird, but I mean, that's the way I thought. That's how much of a purist I was. And then I remember the real icing on the cake was when Doc Souchon sat in and played banjo, and it really pissed me off. And it's a shame, because I mean, Doc was a New Orleanian, but he had done a lot of very good things for people, and he loved the music, and he projected that love for the music. His father saved my father's life. My father had a strangulated hernia, and his father had operated on my father and saved his life. So, I mean, I shouldn't have felt that way at all about Doc Souchon, but I had this young kind of attitude, you know.
Well, a certain idealism there.
What's the word? Mesaic?
Messianic.
Messianic. That's the word I'm looking for, messianic attitude.
Well, so you put this band in front of the jazz club audience. How'd they take to it?

It seemed to me a lot of people liked it, and a lot of people didn't like it. I mean, you either liked it or you didn't like it. A lot of people just thought it was not very good music. And there was a lot of, there was a lot of talk in town. I mean, when you talk to a lot of the white Dixielanders, they always said the older black musicians couldn't really play. They didn't know their instruments. They couldn't play in tune. They couldn't read music. And there was a lot of this kind of bias against black musicians. I know the jazz club
was quite factionalized on the racial issue. Yeah. It was really odd. At least two factions and probably some middle ground too.

So I just kind of remember doing the session and that was kind of the end of my relationship with the jazz club. I can't remember what people actually said at the time and it's really hard for me to, I'm sorry, but it's really hard for me to remember exactly what went down. I wish some of those guys were around. My Percy's still around. Maybe he remembers. I don't know. You know, but I've tried to talk to Percy. I've tried to call him and I've sent him some photographs and stuff and he hasn't answered back. He doesn't want to be bothered with that. Maybe it's not a happy moment
in his life either. Yeah, it could bother you.
But I wished I had the photograph because the photograph is I think a very important document on what I was doing at the time and that it was so unusual.
Yeah.

I mean, if I've done anything in the city, I've done some very unusual things. Now, a lot of people from this town have done, or came here, have done very unusual things, but along the lines of the music. You know?

I'll tell you what, you talked about the Playboy Club and working in the VIP lounge with Al and whatnot, but maybe fill us in on some of your more recent activities since then. I remember the health department closed the Playboy Club down in the mid-70s with 74 or something like that.

Right after that, I went on the road with Jack Jones playing bass. Well, during the interim when I played guitar, like I switched over to the six-string guitar, played six-string guitar for many years, played with a guy by the name of Joe Burton, who Charlie,
I'm sure, remembers. Oh my gosh, yes.
Who had one of the, probably the most visible jazz gigs ever in this town.
That's an epic in itself. It's an epic in itself.
It's a pretty strange one. And by the way,
Piano player? Yeah.

Yeah. By the way, Joe Burton, even though he wasn't a great player, was responsible for getting some of the best bass players and drummers work in town. Reed worked with him quite a while. James Black worked with him quite a while. Charlie, you worked with him, didn't you?
Yeah. Well, he drove all the better drummers away because by that time I was into my English teaching career and he pissed them off so badly that they wouldn't work with him anymore.

But another thing he did. And this goes back to it's very important in New Orleans to have outside influences because what happens, like in the case of Maus, you get these outside influences, they come to the city, Bill Evans is another example, they develop. And they develop, it's a give and take, it's a compromise with the city. They absorb things from the city and the city absorbs things from them. And I think that connection is really important. Anyway, it's kind of New York in a way. It's kind of what's been happening all, you know, somebody, Ellis once said to me, nobody's from New York. You know, it's like New Yorkers are all from somewhere else. You know, in a sense, a lot of the New Orleans scene has been that way too. And a lot of the greatest New Orleans musicians are people who developed here who came from somewhere else, like in the case of Maus and Bill Evans, you know. But, so, oh, talking about Joe Burton, anyway, he comes and he has this gig and he has this club on Canal Street and Jeff Davis. Very nice club. And the thing that he did was bring Jay Cave to town. Jay Cave was a bass player from Philly who had played with Nita Simone, John Erdly, Benny Goodman. He had a lot of experience, excellent musician, excellent bass player, kind of in a Doug Watkins, early Ray Brown mode. Came to town and I, that's my first real introduction other than hearing Chuck Beatty. I hadn't really heard Richie play that much other than hearing Chuck Beatty play at the jazz room, Dominic's jazz room, which is one of those beatnik hangouts we're talking about with Ed Blackwell. Other than hearing Chuck Beatty, I hadn't really heard this kind of bass playing until I heard Jay. And then sitting next to Jay every night and playing like,
you know,

four or five hour gig with him was really an education and really taught me more about bass than anybody I studied with. And that's when I really became interested in playing upright bass and that's when I switched over right around that time. And then started all the things that happened at the Playboy Club, started playing with Buddy Prima and so on, again on bass at this time,
you know.
So by that time, Charlie, I think you were out of town, weren't you?

I went, excuse me, I was in the army for a while while he was, right around that time when you started playing with Burton. Then I came back and he had alienated a lot of the musicians and I'd work with him occasionally. In fact, my paycheck was being held up by the state of Louisiana during the integration time and if that hadn't been for Joe Burton, giving me a few bucks a night would be terrible. When I was at his club I would not have had money to feed my family at that time. But yeah, I was out of town for part of that but I was here doing a lot of Joe Burton's epic, as it were. He was more of a promoter and a self-promoter than a musician although he could have been a fine piano player but he was more interested in thrusting his ego around the place than in getting into the artistry and he hired good musicians as long as he could keep them.
He hired them and fuss at them.
Incredible.
Better musicians than him.
Am I raging? No, he was like a real idiot.
I seem to remember something about him ending up with a television show in the area

or something like that. He had a television show out of here. In fact, there's a famous thing where he's writing the staff and just like an educational show on music and what jazz is and so on. And he's writing the staff on a blackboard and he writes six lines and Jay is over in the corner saying,
you know.
And then there's the famous thing. He also had a television show in the evening. I don't know if you remember that.

I played one of his shows. I've forgotten. He had that. I know he'd promote like crazy and he'd always blow it financially and then he'd get somebody else to back him and then he'd get a TV show and a radio show.

Always getting involved in these schemes where you owe people money and then he was in danger and then he'd close the club suddenly and then it would open again. And his wife was always attempting suicide. I remember when I was there she attempted suicide one night in the ladies room.
Well,

people wouldn't deliver. He'd talk about this over his radio. The famous Dick Martin show was on at that time. Well, he used to have a show right after that. Right after the Dick Martin show. And it was kind of a late hours jazz show and it was punctuated with his comments to his wife. she had some problems with narcotics and he'd be saying things like, Leah! Her name was Leah. Are you doing those pills again? Put those pills away! I mean, you'd hear like a little noodling at the piano and then you'd hear the screaming about, put those pills away, you know.
This was a radio show?

Yeah, this was on radio. Live radio show. Yeah, it was incredible. And then we started doing these television shows and I remember one television show we did had Liston Johnson. Do you know who Liston is? Liston is like just a legend in himself, man. I mean, he's been around for so many years. He's one of those early people who came to New Orleans and absorbed the culture and stayed here and, I mean, was a fixture at the Fairmont for how many years, man? When it was way back when it was at Roosevelt and the Fountain Lounge. Anyway, Liston was playing tenor on this particular radio show and that morning Stan, the headline had a picture of Stan Getz robbing a drugstore in L.A. or somewhere in California and Liston was taking a chorus and Joe screams, this is on television, Joe screams from the piano, you must rob drugstores. So this is the kind of guy he was, man, really out. Anyway, but I got to, I got to, like, as I said, play guitar every night which was really important I think for my guitar development plus being, sitting next to Jay and that was really a catalyst for me taking up the upright bass and subsequently I went and played a lot with Al Baleto and played at the Playboy Clubs with these various great piano players like Rusty and like John Probst, Dave West and people who, you know,

segments.title: Opening and voice check at the Hogan Jazz Archive
segments.summary: Rayburn opens the 1992 joint interview with Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor; both give birth dates and places.

segments.title: New Orleans' indifference to music as a profession
segments.summary: Huntington says the city treats music as not a real job, even for a middle-aged player today.

segments.title: Start of reel two
segments.summary: Reel change; Rayburn asks Suhor to expand on 1950s-60s modern jazz players.

segments.title: Suhor's list of New Orleans modern jazz innovators and where they played
segments.summary: Suhor names Ed Blackwell, Mouse, Earl Palmer and others as leaders, and the quarter dungeons and Texas Lounge where they played; Huntington adds comments on Ellis.

segments.title: Lou Dillon the teacher and more modern players
segments.summary: Suhor credits drummer Lou Dillon as a teacher who shaped Reed and himself and whose methods he used teaching Johnny Vidacovich; more names are listed.

segments.title: Huntington's isolation as a young player and friendship with Buddy Prima
segments.summary: With no peer group, immersed among older black musicians, he drank and became a recluse; Buddy Prima befriended him and played a big role.

segments.title: Americana and third stream with Prima, Suhor and friends; shift from guitar to bass
segments.summary: Peers in the rhythm section and modern classical interests, John Butler's teaching, WWL radio shows, R&B drudgery on guitar, and Roy Montrell and Blackwell playing on a truck.

segments.title: Playboy Club, Al Boleto and integration
segments.summary: Boleto built a modern jazz room with several bands, pushed integration at risk of arrest, and Marshall Smith brought Ellis to hear Huntington.

segments.title: Suhor on Huntington's roots among older black players
segments.summary: Suhor praises Huntington's deep traditional roots; Huntington says older black players embodied what he wanted to hear, with a reaction against white music.

segments.title: Organizing the integrated band at the New Orleans Jazz Club
segments.summary: Huntington, about 16, brought Cie Frazier, Percy and others to the Roosevelt; guests like George Gerard, Jack Delaney and Doc Souchon joined, which irked his purist attitude.

segments.title: Reaction to the Jazz Club session and the surviving photograph
segments.summary: Audience opinion was split and the club factionalized; Huntington recalls little and wishes he had the photograph.

segments.title: Joe Burton's club gig and its bass and drum players
segments.summary: After the Playboy Club closed Huntington played six-string with pianist Joe Burton, whose gig employed many top drummers and bassists.

segments.title: Outside influences in New Orleans and Jay Cave on bass
segments.summary: Huntington argues outsiders enrich the city, and says bassist Jay Cave, brought by Burton, taught him upright bass.

segments.title: Suhor on Burton's character and his own army absence
segments.summary: Suhor was in the army during this time, worked with Burton occasionally, and describes him as a self-promoter who drove musicians away.

segments.title: Burton's television and radio shows and later bass work
segments.summary: Stories of Burton's TV and radio shows, his wife Leah, and Liston Johnson; Huntington then moves into bass at the Playboy Clubs.
